name: Delft Blue
basis: why: earthenware in white tin glaze painted in cobalt, built up in layers; how: strokes along isophotes, repeated passes in darks, crackle

lumenary.blurb: Dutch Delftware: cobalt painted onto white tin glaze with a fine brush. The strokes follow the form, darker where the picture is darker, and the whole glaze is hair-cracked with age.

why: Delftware was the Dutch answer to the Chinese porcelain that ships brought to Europe. It is ordinary earthenware dressed up with white tin glaze and painted in cobalt blue. The painter’s brush follows the form of the thing, and darker passages are built up by going over them more than once, so blue builds into shadow in layers.
how: Blur the picture heavily to a smooth brightness field F.
At every point, find the direction along which F does not change, perpendicular to its gradient, and lay strokes along those lines so they curve round shapes.
Scatter seeds on a jittered grid and shuffle them.
In each layer, paint at a seed only if the brightness there is below a threshold that starts at 0.70 and falls by 0.17 for each layer, so dark places are painted over several times.
Add outlines, glaze crackle and, if chosen, a plate shape with a rim.
history: Dutch potters in Delft developed blue and white earthenware in the seventeenth century, in imitation of Ming porcelain imported by the Dutch East India Company. De Koninklijke Porceleyne Fles, founded in 1653, is still producing Delftware today. Windmills, tulips and landscapes remain popular subjects.
uses: Illustration with a limited blue palette
terms: Tin-glazed earthenware made in and around Delft.
Pottery fired at a low temperature, which stays slightly porous.
The direction in which brightness changes fastest.
paragraphs: Delftware was the Dutch answer to Chinese porcelain in the seventeenth century. It is earthenware coated with white tin glaze and painted in cobalt before the glaze is fired. The painter’s brush follows the form of the thing being drawn, and darker passages are built up by going over them more than once. The program does the same. It blurs your picture heavily to a smooth brightness field F, finds at every point the direction along which F does not change, which is perpendicular to its gradient, and lays strokes along those lines so they curve round shapes.

Seeds are scattered on a jittered grid and shuffled. In each of the layers a seed paints only if the brightness there is below a threshold that falls from 0.70 by 0.17 for each layer, so a dark place is painted over several times and a light place once or not at all. A stroke follows the field in both directions for the chosen length, flipping the field’s sign when needed so that it keeps going the same way. The plate has a painted rim of ticks and dots between rings, a soft highlight on the glaze, and a net of cracks from Worley noise, 16 px across, bent slightly so that the lines are not straight.

equations.tex: \mathbf t=\frac{\big(-\partial_y F,\ \partial_x F\big)}{\lVert\nabla F\rVert},\qquad \mathbf x_{n+1}=\mathbf x_n+\Delta\,\mathbf t(\mathbf x_n)
equations.note: A stroke follows the isophote, the line of equal brightness. Δ is 2.6 px and the sign of t is chosen to agree with the previous step. Where the gradient is nearly zero a fixed angle of about 0.7 radians takes over.
Layer ℓ threshold, tested on T, a lightly blurred brightness (the heavy blur F only steers the strokes). ξ is a random number per seed, so the limit is a little ragged.
The darker the place, the more opaque and the wider the stroke.

presets.text: Full-sheet mode shows the picture without the plate rim.
Long strokes follow the form like an engraver’s line.
